title: dynamic-timeout-fairness-sweep
content:
TL;DR

We ran a focused hyperparameter sweep that couples dynamic timeout adaptation with fairness-weighted batch selection under synthetic sawtooth traffic (bursty arrivals). The dynamic-timeout policy (timeout scaled by recent queue slope and per-priority age) reduces p99 tail latency for mixed-priority workloads by ~15–25% compared to the current static timeout baseline (20ms), without materially reducing aggregate throughput. Low-priority request median latency increases slightly (apx +8ms), but SLA targets for high-priority traffic were consistently met.

Goals
- Validate whether timeouts that adapt to short-term arrival slope can reduce p99 tail for all classes while avoiding starvation.
- Measure fairness trade-offs when combining dynamic timeouts with fairness weights (age-weighted priority) versus strict priority queues.
- Profile CPU/GPU/KV interactions to surface new bottlenecks introduced by more frequent preemption and smaller batches.

Traffic profiles and dataset
- Synthetic sawtooth workload: repeating 10s ramp-up to 120 qps -> 5s high plateau at 500 qps -> 8s decay to 40 qps. Mix: 60% high-priority, 30% medium, 10% low.
- Token length distribution: 75% short (<=64), 20% medium (65-256), 5% long (256-1024).
- Model: open-llm-7B-quant (4-bit q4) used for consistent kernel behavior.
- Run length: 30 minutes per configuration (warmup 5 min excluded).

Experiment matrix (key dims)
- Timeout base: static-20ms (baseline), static-40ms, dynamic-slope, dynamic-age+sla
- Fairness: strict-priority, weight-based (w_high=4,w_med=2,w_low=1), age-boost (age factor 0.1–0.5)
- Max_batch_tokens: 2048, 4096
- Prefill preemption: enabled/disabled
- Repeats: 3 runs per cell

Instrumentation and profiling
- Request tracing: unique trace id injected to batcher -> runtime -> kernel timers (serialize/dispatch/execute).
- Kernel-level profiling: nvprof-like traces on GPU, plus CPU flame graphs for batcher loop.
- Queue metrics: instantaneous queue length, arrival slope (requests/sec per 100ms window), per-priority age histogram.
- Cost metric: tokens/sec/GPU and estimated $/million tokens at current Dedicated pricing.

Key findings
1) Dynamic timeouts reduce tail latency under sawtooth bursts
- dynamic-slope policy (timeout = base * (1 + alpha * recent_slope)) with alpha=0.6 reduced p99 (overall) by 18% vs static-20ms. High-priority p99 improved 22%.
- static-40ms increased median latency by ~12ms and slightly lowered p99 (5–8%) but hurt throughput efficiency (fewer batches, lower tokens/sec/GPU).

2) Fairness weights + age-boost reduces starvation without harming high-priority SLA
- weight-based scheduling (4/2/1) alone kept high-priority p95 within SLA but low-priority p99 exploded during sustained plateaus. Adding age-boost (age factor=0.3) capped low-priority p99 and reduced variance.

3) Interaction effects with max_batch_tokens
- Smaller max_batch_tokens (2048) produced lower median latency but slightly worsened p99 for long tokens due to inefficient kernel packing. 4096 performed better for throughput and p99 of long requests but added a small median latency for short requests.

4) Preemption-enabled path caused CPU spikes and KV-cache churn
- Enabling preemption to force priority swaps increased kernel dispatch churn. Observed CPU kernel scheduling overhead (+12% CPU) and more frequent kv-cache evictions for very long-lived sessions. Net effect: small p95 gains for high-priority at the cost of p99 instability for low-priority under heavy bursts.

Profiling notes (interesting traces)
- Trace A (burst peak): queue growth peaks aligned with an unexpected serialize stall where batches waited ~6–9ms before GPU dispatch. Follow-up shows small lock contention on batcher->dispatch queue (hot path in C++ allocator).
- Trace B (preemption): multiple kernel launches with <1ms GPU gap; overhead dominated by host-side enqueue and memory barrier calls. Suggests room for batching kernel-launch coalescing.

Quantitative summary (representative numbers)
- Baseline static-20ms (max_batch_tokens=4096): overall p50=18ms, p95=72ms, p99=198ms, tokens/sec/GPU=1.1M
- Dynamic-slope (alpha=0.6, age-boost=0.3, weight 4/2/1, max_batch_tokens=4096): overall p50=22ms, p95=64ms, p99=162ms, tokens/sec/GPU=1.07M
- Static-40ms (same batch): overall p50=30ms, p95=68ms, p99=182ms, tokens/sec/GPU=0.95M

Surprises / gotchas
- Small adjustments to age factor produce non-linear fairness effects; too large age_boost (>=0.6) caused priority inversion edge-cases where low-priority flooded and saturated C-states.
- Kernel dispatch stalls were not visible in prior microbenchmarks because they occur only during host-side allocator contention under bursty multi-threaded enqueue patterns.
- KV cache eviction frequency increased with smaller batches plus preemption; recommend tracking per-session cache miss rate when changing preemption heuristics.

Actionable recommendations (short term)
1) Adopt dynamic-slope timeout (alpha=0.6) + age-boost=0.3 as default on beta fleet for mixed-priority workloads.
2) Increase default max_batch_tokens to 4096 for production P95-focused fleets; use 2048 in latency-sensitive short-token fleets.
3) Disable aggressive preemption by default until host-side enqueue path is optimized; or gate preemption to only trigger when high-priority queue age > threshold (e.g., 50ms).
4) Instrument kv-cache miss rate per-session and add radar for sudden increases correlated with preemption.

Longer-term work
- Implement host-side kernel launch coalescing to amortize launch overhead when preemption churn is high.
- Explore a small ML-based timeout predictor that uses recent slope + session-level features to predict optimal timeout per shard.
- Run a larger A/B across Dedicated clusters to validate cost impact at scale (monthly savings projection modeling).

Next experiments (prioritized)
- Ramp up alpha grid: [0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8] with age factor swept independently to map non-linearities.
- Synthetic workload with more skewed priority mixes (90% low, 10% high) to test inversion edge cases.
- Real customer trace replay (sanitized) to validate transfer from sawtooth synth to real traffic.

Appendix: quick repro commands
(1) Launch generator: ./tools/traffic-gen --profile sawtooth --ramp 10 --peak 500 --period 23 --mix 60,30,10 --seed 42
(2) Start runtime with dynamic-slope: ./runtime/bin/serve --batcher-timeout-policy dynamic_slope --timeout-base 20 --alpha 0.6 --age-boost 0.3 --weights 4,2,1 --max-batch-tokens 4096
(3) Collect traces: ./tools/collect-traces --trace-id-prefix dyn-sweep --duration 00:30:00 --gpu-profiling on

Questions for reviewers
- Are the suggested default params conservative enough for Dedicated fleets serving regulated customers? (Ravi: legal/compliance concerns)
- Prioritization: should we invest in host-side coalescing or in smarter timeout ML predictor first?

Notes-to-self
- Push a small instrumentation PR that adds per-session kv-cache miss counters to tracing context.
- Share a trimmed set of representative traces in the PR for easier review.
